curriculum.lesson_evidence: In drama, a role is a person or creature you pretend to be. A character is built from traits, such as brave, shy or grumpy, and from what the character wants. You show a character through your body (how you stand and move), your face and your voice. Staying in role means you keep acting as the character until the teacher or leader says to stop. Drama is pretend and safe, with no hitting or real touching. You can always step out of a role or describe it if you do not want to act.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Create a character who is a nervous new student. Choose two traits and say how you would show them with your body, face and voice.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Traits: shy and worried. Body: hunched shoulders, looking at the floor. Face: eyes wide, small smile. Voice: quiet and a little shaky.' It links each trait to a physical choice, which makes a character believable.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that drama means just acting silly or copying someone from TV. Acting means making deliberate choices about a character's traits so the audience can believe in them.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Make three characters: a king, a robot and a shy mouse. For each write two traits, a way of standing and moving, a face and a voice. Perform one for a family member who guesses the traits. You may describe instead of performing.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: Zoe plays an old fisherman. She decides his traits are patient and tired. She walks slowly with a bent back, speaks in a low, slow voice and sighs. Her character wants to catch one last fish. Everyone can tell the character's traits from her body and voice, and she keeps in role until the teacher says 'freeze and thank you'.

TRY FIRST
Create a character who is a nervous new student. Choose two traits and say how you would show them with your body, face and voice.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Traits: shy and worried. Body: hunched shoulders, looking at the floor. Face: eyes wide, small smile. Voice: quiet and a little shaky.' It links each trait to a physical choice, which makes a character believable.
teach_steps.explain:
In drama, a role is a person or creature you pretend to be. A character is built from traits, such as brave, shy or grumpy, and from what the character wants. You show a character through your body (how you stand and move), your face and your voice. Staying in role means you keep acting as the character until the teacher or leader says to stop. Drama is pretend and safe, with no hitting or real touching. You can always step out of a role or describe it if you do not want to act.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.
